procedural_history.impugned_order: Final Judgment and Order dated 05.09.2023 of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in CRLRA No. 410 of 2022, which dismissed the Criminal Revision Application and effectively dismissed the discharge application.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The Appellant preferred a Criminal Revision Application before the High Court after the Trial Court rejected their discharge application. The High Court dismissed the Revision Application.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Appellant challenged the High Court's order before the Supreme Court because the High Court dismissed the Revision Application, effectively denying the discharge application. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and allowed the application for discharge.

directions: Impugned order of the High Court is set aside.
The application for discharge is allowed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the alleged conduct of the appellant-accused in the nature of marital disputes prima facie attracts Section 306 of the IPC, read with Section 107 of the IPC, to continue the proceedings of the Trial Court against the appellant.

facts: The appellant is the wife of the deceased, who committed suicide by hanging.
The deceased's mother filed an FIR, alleging the appellant harassed and beat the deceased for money and for the transfer of their jointly owned house into her name.
Further allegations included the appellant sending vulgar messages, insisting the deceased not visit his parents, and creating a ruckus at his office.
The charge sheet filed by the police accused the appellant of harassing the deceased over money and property, thereby inducing him to attempt suicide.
The Trial Court and the High Court had both previously dismissed the appellant's applications for discharge from the case.
law: To establish an offense under Section 306 of the IPC (abetment of suicide), it must be read with Section 107, which defines abetment.
Abetment requires either instigation, conspiracy, or intentional aid in the commission of the act.
For a conviction, there must be a clear 'mens rea' (guilty intent) and a positive, direct act by the accused that instigates or aids the suicide.
A proximate link must exist between the accused's actions and the suicide. Mere allegations of harassment are insufficient without a positive act close to the time of the event.
The court must find that the cruelty and harassment were so severe that they left the victim with no other alternative but to end their life.
application: The Supreme Court applied the strict legal requirements for abetment to the facts of this marital dispute.
It found that the three essential ingredients of abetment under Section 107 IPC (instigation, conspiracy, or aid) were not present in the appellant's alleged conduct.
The Court concluded there was no proximate link between the marital disputes and the deceased's decision to commit suicide.

It specifically noted the absence of any active role or positive/direct act by the appellant to instigate or aid the suicide. There was no allegation that she had ever suggested suicide to the deceased.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the alleged conduct of the appellant, which stemmed from marital disputes, did not prima facie constitute abetment of suicide under Section 306 read with Section 107 of the IPC. The Court found that the high legal threshold of a direct, positive act with a clear intent to drive the deceased to suicide was not met, and therefore, the criminal proceedings against the appellant could not continue.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the alleged conduct of the appellant-accused in the nature of marital disputes prima facie attracts Section 306 of the IPC, read with Section 107 of the IPC, to continue the proceedings of the Trial Court against the appellant.
appellant_arguments: There is no evidence showing an active role played by the Appellant which has abetted the commission of suicide.
The dwelling house was jointly purchased by the Appellant and the deceased, and therefore there was no question of insisting to transfer the house in the name of the Appellant.
respondent_arguments: The ingredients essential for the offence under Section 306 IPC were clearly made out from the evidence collected during the investigation.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: To establish an offense under Section 306 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), the accused's actions must satisfy one of the three criteria for "abetment" as defined in Section 107 IPC: instigation, engagement in a conspiracy, or intentional aid in the commission of the act.
obiter: Before holding an accused guilty of an offence under Section 306 IPC, the court must scrupulously examine the facts and circumstances of the case and assess the evidence to determine if the legal requirements are met.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court found that none of the three essential ingredients of abetment as defined in Section 107 of the IPC—instigation, engagement, or intentional aid—were present in the appellant's alleged conduct. Therefore, the actions of the appellant did not prima facie attract the offense of abetment of suicide under Section 306 of the IPC.
legal_tests_applied: To establish an offense under Section 306 of the IPC (abetment of suicide), the case must satisfy one of the three criteria for "abetment" laid out in Section 107 of the IPC: 1) Instigating any person to do that thing; or 2) Engaging in any conspiracy for the doing of that thing; or 3) Intentionally aiding, by any act or illegal omission, the doing of that thing.

Courts must scrupulously examine the facts and circumstances of the case and assess the evidence to determine if the ingredients of abetment are met before holding an accused guilty under Section 306 IPC.
